blueprint_topic: Management of Care — multidisciplinary liver-transplant evaluation, psychosocial assessment, caregiver support, adherence, and modifiable barriers
stem: During liver-transplant evaluation, a client asks, "Why does the team need to discuss my mental health, medication adherence, and caregiver plan in addition to my medical tests?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: These factors help identify modifiable barriers, assess adherence and support needs, and plan interventions that can improve transplant safety and success.
options.B: These factors are used mainly to predict who will follow instructions; treatment of mental-health or support problems is generally deferred until after transplant.
options.C: Once medical testing shows acceptable surgical risk, psychosocial findings are documented for discharge planning but have little role in pretransplant planning.
options.D: A past psychiatric diagnosis is treated as evidence of poor adherence, so the assessment mainly confirms whether the client meets psychosocial exclusion criteria.

rationale: A is correct. The current AASLD/AST guideline includes psychosocial evaluation as a core component of adult liver-transplant candidate assessment. It recommends evaluating reasonable expectations for adherence and mental-health stability, assessing adequate caregiver/social support for the wait-list and postoperative period, and identifying strategies to mitigate social or financial barriers. The guideline states that the purpose of psychosocial assessment is to identify areas requiring intervention and to develop strategies or treatments that support successful transplantation. B is incorrect because identified psychosocial problems are not simply deferred until after transplant; the guideline emphasizes addressing modifiable issues before transplantation and reassessing as needed. C is incorrect because psychosocial findings are part of pretransplant candidate evaluation and planning, not merely post-transplant discharge planning. D is incorrect because a psychiatric history is not equivalent to poor adherence or automatic exclusion; the guideline states that mental-health disorders, even serious ones, are not absolute contraindications when appropriate treatment, stability, and support can be achieved.
educational_objective: Explain that psychosocial and caregiver assessment is a core part of liver-transplant evaluation used to identify modifiable barriers, assess adherence and support needs, and develop interventions that promote safe wait-list and post-transplant care without treating mental-health history as an automatic exclusion.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) and American Society of Transplantation (AST)
source_document_title: AASLD AST Practice Guideline on Adult Liver Transplantation: Candidate Evaluation
source_version_date: Epub December 17, 2025; Hepatology June 1, 2026; current guideline rechecked 2026-08-20
source_locator: AASLD/AST guideline — 'The Psychosocial Evaluation,' Question 16. Guideline Statement 35: adherence to medical directives and mental-health stability; Statement 36: adequate social/caregiver support and mitigation of social/financial barriers; Statement 42: access to appropriate mental-health evaluation/treatment. 'Rationale and Background': goal is to identify psychosocial areas requiring intervention and assist with strategies/treatments; domains include adherence, caregiver support, cognitive capacity, psychiatric/substance-use issues, illness/treatment understanding, coping, and practical caregiver functions. Section 3, Guideline Statement 46 and Psychosocial discussion: mental-health disorders, even serious ones, are not absolute contraindications; treatment/stabilization and reassessment should be pursued when feasible.
source_claim_supported: The current AASLD/AST guideline directly supports comprehensive psychosocial evaluation of adherence, mental-health stability, caregiver/social support, treatment understanding, and modifiable social/financial barriers as part of liver-transplant candidate assessment, with interventions and reassessment rather than automatic exclusion based on psychiatric diagnosis alone.
blueprint_locator: Management of Care, overview printed page 7 / PDF file page index 10: identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members and assess need for referrals/orders. Appendix A Management of Care, printed page 21 / PDF file page index 24: Collaboration with Multidisciplinary Team includes identifying significant information to report to other disciplines and reviewing the plan of care for continuity; Concepts of Management includes coordinating/managing care and acting as liaison between client and others.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the original longest-key cue and the 'only' distractor pattern. The final choices are tightly length-balanced and test realistic misconceptions: treating psychosocial evaluation as prediction without pretransplant intervention, relegating it to discharge planning, and equating psychiatric history with exclusion/poor adherence. Post-fetch adversarial reread found no further defect requiring another rewrite.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly reflects the guideline's purpose of identifying psychosocial barriers, assessing adherence/support, and developing interventions to improve transplant readiness and outcomes.
option_audit.B: Plausible prediction-only misconception; incorrect because the guideline emphasizes intervention, treatment, mitigation, and reassessment before transplantation rather than deferring psychosocial problems until afterward.
option_audit.C: Plausible medical-first misconception; incorrect because psychosocial assessment is a defined component of candidate evaluation and pretransplant planning.
option_audit.D: Plausible stigma/exclusion misconception; incorrect because psychiatric diagnosis alone does not establish poor adherence and even serious mental-health disorders are not absolute contraindications when treatable/stabilizable with adequate support.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type distractor absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are tightly balanced: A 155, B 163, C 160, D 162 characters; the key is the shortest rather than uniquely longest.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives explain the purpose and implications of psychosocial/caregiver assessment using parallel transplant-evaluation language.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after post-fetch adversarial reread. B, C, and D each contradict a specific current guideline principle.
